claims.text: Maintenance of a single-phase solid solution in equimolar multimetallic nanoparticles is governed by the interplay of high configurational entropy and sluggish atomic diffusion.
When configurational entropy dominates and diffusion remains slow, the nanoparticles preserve a uniform single-phase structure.
Thermal energy or reactive environments can lower kinetic barriers and thereby cause localized elemental segregation and secondary-phase formation.
The starting nanoparticles contain five or more metals at near-equiatomic ratios and are initially a single-phase solid solution.
In situ diffraction, electron microscopy, and elemental mapping can track structural and compositional stability during heating.
Extended exposure or reactive gases are conditions expected to compromise diffusion barriers.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically favors formation or retention of a single solid-solution phase.
Lattice distortions and severe atomic-size mismatches create high atomic-diffusion barriers in these nanoparticles.
High diffusion barriers inhibit atomic rearrangement and elemental segregation.
Once thermal energy overcomes the diffusion barriers, the solid solution can decompose locally.
Under controlled inert conditions, the nanoparticles will retain a single-phase structure up to 1923 K.
Under controlled inert conditions, the nanoparticles will retain a uniform elemental distribution up to 1923 K.
Reactive environments or extended high-temperature annealing will produce earlier elemental segregation or secondary phases relative to the initial state.
The exact temperature and time required to overcome kinetic barriers depend on elemental combination and operating environment.
Segregation or secondary-phase formation in an inert environment well below 1923 K, without an expected reduction in kinetic barriers, would falsify the hypothesis.
Retention of the single-phase structure under conditions known to lower diffusion barriers would falsify the proposed mechanism.
